verses.text: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, saying,

“Take a scroll of a book, and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah, even to this day.
It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I purpose to do to them; that they may each return from his evil way; that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah; and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all Yahweh’s words, which he had spoken to him, on a scroll of a book.
Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying, “I am restricted. I can’t go into Yahweh’s house.

Therefore you go, and read from the scroll, which you have written from my mouth, Yahweh’s words in the ears of the people in Yahweh’s house on the fast day. Also you shall read them in the ears of all Judah who come out of their cities.
It may be they will present their supplication before Yahweh, and will each return from his evil way; for Yahweh has pronounced great anger and wrath against this people.”
Baruch the son of Neriah did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book Yahweh’s words in Yahweh’s house.

Now in the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem, and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem, proclaimed a fast before Yahweh.

Then Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the book in Yahweh’s house, in the room of Gemariah the son of Shaphan, the scribe, in the upper court, at the entry of the new gate of Yahweh’s house, in the ears of all the people.
When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, had heard out of the book all Yahweh’s words,

he went down into the king’s house, into the scribe’s room: and behold, all the princes were sitting there, Elishama the scribe, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes.
Then Micaiah declared to them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the book in the ears of the people.

Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, to Baruch, saying, “Take in your hand the scroll in which you have read in the ears of the people, and come.” So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand, and came to them.
They said to him, “Sit down now, and read it in our hearing.” So Baruch read it in their hearing.
Now when they had heard all the words, they turned in fear one toward another, and said to Baruch, “We will surely tell the king of all these words.”
They asked Baruch, saying, “Tell us now, How did you write all these words at his mouth?”
Then Baruch answered them, “He dictated all these words to me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book.”
Then the princes said to Baruch, “You and Jeremiah go hide. Don’t let anyone know where you are.”
They went in to the king into the court; but they had laid up the scroll in the room of Elishama the scribe; and they told all the words in the ears of the king.
So the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll; and he took it out of the room of Elishama the scribe. Jehudi read it in the ears of the king, and in the ears of all the princes who stood beside the king.
Now the king was sitting in the winter house in the ninth month: and there was a fire in the brazier burning before him.
When Jehudi had read three or four leaves, the king cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was in the brazier, until all the scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the brazier.
The king and his servants who heard all these words were not afraid, and didn’t tear their garments.
Moreover Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the scroll; but he would not listen to them.
The king commanded Jerahmeel the king’s son, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet; but Yahweh hid them.
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah, after the king had burned the scroll, and the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah, saying,
“Take again another scroll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.

Concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, ‘Yahweh says: “You have burned this scroll, saying, “Why have you written therein, saying, ‘The king of Babylon shall certainly come and destroy this land, and shall cause to cease from there man and animal?’”’
Therefore Yahweh says concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: “He will have no one to sit on David’s throne. His dead body will be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost.

I will punish him and his offspring  and his servants for their iniquity; and I will bring on them, on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and on the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them, but they didn’t listen.”’”

Then took Jeremiah another scroll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire; and many similar words were added to them.

footnotes.content: The Lord called Jeremiah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim—a king who would prove hostile to His word. Notice how the Lord speaks in plainness: 'This word came to Jeremiah.' When heaven makes a move, it comes with purpose, not confusion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God commands Jeremiah to write every word spoken since Josiah's reign—decades of prophecy now fixed in ink on scroll. There's grace in this: the word, once written, cannot be lost even if speakers fade or hearers forget.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the Lord's hope: 'It may be they will return.' He never stops offering the door of repentance, even to a stiff-necked people. The wording itself—'forgive their iniquity and their sin'—shows Him holding both the judgment and the mercy in His hands at once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah could not write it himself—he called Baruch. This tells us something: faithful witness sometimes works through partnership, not solo heroics. Baruch became the scribe, the one who held the pen, which meant he held the weight of every word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah says plainly: 'I am restricted. I can't go into Yahweh's house.' No complaint, no self-pity—just the fact. There are times the Lord bars His own servants from certain doors, and wisdom is knowing when to hand the work to another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah sends Baruch to read on a fast day, when hearts might be tender and listening. He seeks out the people in the Temple courts and those who traveled from the cities—casting the net wide so none can claim they never heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hope again: 'It may be they will present their supplication.' The prophet doesn't assume hardness; he leaves the door cracked open for repentance, knowing the Lord's anger can be turned aside by those who truly turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baruch obeyed without hesitation: 'did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him.' Obedience is often less dramatic than we expect—a man with a scroll, reading in a court, trusting the Lord's word to do its work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A year has passed—now in the fifth year, in the ninth month, Jerusalem proclaims a fast. The people gather at the Temple. The scene is set; the listeners are assembled. The Lord's timing is not ours, but it is always purposeful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baruch reads in Gemariah's room, at the Temple's new gate, before all the people. The location matters—it's not a secret whisper but a public reading in the Lord's house itself, where His word belongs and where it can reach many ears at once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Micaiah, Gemariah's son, hears the whole of Yahweh's words. One person listening fully—really listening—becomes the bridge between the prophet's voice and the powers that be. The Lord often moves through a single attentive ear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Micaiah hurries down to the king's house, where the princes sit in the scribe's room. Notice the officials gathered: Elishama, Delaiah, Elnathan, Gemariah, Zedekiah. These are the kingdom's counselors, and news reaches them through a young man's faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Micaiah declares everything he heard when Baruch read aloud. He doesn't distort or summarize for advantage—he reports the whole counsel of God. This is what an honest witness does: carries the message intact, even knowing its power to disturb.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes send for Baruch and the scroll. He comes without resistance—the scribe holding God's words, moving quietly through Jerusalem's halls. When believers obey, even in uncertainty, the Lord sees and moves the pieces where they need to be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes ask Baruch to sit and read to them. It's formal, respectful—the authorities treating the scroll with ceremony. For a moment, the word of God has their full attention, and they listen without interruption.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After hearing all the words, the princes 'turned in fear one toward another.' For an instant, the Lord's judgment touches their hearts. They know they must tell the king—the burden of the message compels them, even though telling the king may not end well.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes ask Baruch the origin of these words: 'How did you write all these words at his mouth?' They want to be sure—is this truly the prophet's voice, or a scribe's invention? The question shows they understand: written words carry weight and demand authority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baruch answers plainly: 'He dictated all these words to me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink.' No embellishment, no defense—just the simple chain of faithfulness from Jeremiah's lips to Baruch's pen. The truth is the answer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes warn Baruch and Jeremiah: 'Go hide. Don't let anyone know where you are.' These officials, afraid themselves now, show a flicker of mercy. They know the king will not take this word well, and they do what little they can to protect the messengers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes go to the king but first hide the scroll in Elishama's room—a small act of preservation, perhaps hoping he might yet be merciful. They tell him everything, laying the words before him, and now the weight passes to the king's shoulders.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king sends Jehudi to fetch the scroll. Now it comes from the scribe's safe-keeping into the king's hand. Jehoiakim reads it aloud—not in secret but before all his princes, as if bearing witness to what he is about to do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king sits in his winter house, with a brazier burning before him. It's a comfortable, private scene—a king in his warmth, untroubled. The detail sets the stage for what he is about to do with the scroll.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three or four leaves read, and Jehoiakim takes his penknife and cuts the scroll, casting it piece by piece into the fire. It's deliberate, slow—not a sudden rage but a calculated destruction. He burns the Lord's word as if he could burn away judgment itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king and his servants do not fear. They don't tear their garments in dread or repentance. The word falls on hard soil. Sometimes people hear God's voice and simply choose not to listen, not to believe, not to bend.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three of the princes—Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah—intercede with the king, begging him not to burn the scroll. There's courage in this: they speak against the king's will, knowing it may cost them. They see what's right and say it anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king commands the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, sending soldiers to seize them. But 'Yahweh hid them.' In the moment when danger closes in, the Lord's hand moves first, tucking His servants into safety. The scroll may burn, but the messengers live.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the burning, Yahweh's word came to Jeremiah again. The king thought he could silence God by burning paper, but the Lord speaks afresh. His words cannot be cut or consumed—they stand eternal, beyond the reach of any penknife or brazier.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God tells Jeremiah: 'Take again another scroll, and write in it all the former words.' What the king destroyed, the Lord replaces. There is a stubborn grace here—the Lord will not be thwarted by human refusal. The work continues.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God gives Jeremiah a message for Jehoiakim: 'You have burned this scroll, saying...' The Lord answers the king's deed. Jehoiakim thought he was protecting his kingdom; the Lord sees it as rebellion, as one man's small defiance against the Almighty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The consequence is spoken: Jehoiakim will have no heir to sit on David's throne. His body will be cast out, scorched by day and frozen by night. Burning the scroll was the last free choice he made; what follows flows from his rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The judgment extends beyond the king: he, his offspring, his servants, all Jerusalem—all will feel the weight of the evil Yahweh pronounced. 'They didn't listen' is the refrain. Judgment is the Lord's final word when mercy is refused over and over.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch, who wrote again. 'Many similar words were added to them.' Readers today hear an echo in this: when one door closes, the Lord opens another. What seems lost in fire becomes fuller, richer, more rooted when written anew by faithful hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
